conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and today I’ll be checking in with you using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS**—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a way to see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll go at your pace. I’ll ask ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one can be answered in just a sentence or two.  

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:  

Over the last seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Lately I feel like I can’t really laugh much at all. It’s not that I never smile, but even the things that used to crack me up just feel kind of flat now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Honestly… not really. I might force a little chuckle if someone else is laughing, but it feels kind of fake. Nothing seems very funny anymore—just one more thing that reminds me I’m not myself.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I still get a tiny spark when I think about maybe grabbing coffee with a friend, but most of the time I don’t even want to plan anything because it feels like it’ll just be too hard or I won’t enjoy it anyway.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or I can’t get her to nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m just not a good mom. I know, rationally, babies cry, but the voice in my head still says, “You should’ve figured this out by now.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s too hot, or maybe she’s not breathing right, or I’ll picture her slipping out of my arms. There’s no real reason—it’s just this constant hum of worry I can’t switch off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week it hit me hard—like my chest gets tight and I feel I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s actually happening; it’s just this sudden wave of dread that something awful is about to happen to the baby or that I’ll mess everything up.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll be trying to fold laundry while she’s napping and suddenly think about the bottles that need sterilizing, the pediatrician appointment to schedule, the texts I haven’t answered…and my chest gets heavy like I’m drowning in little tasks I can’t keep up with.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s happened several nights this week. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with worries—did I fasten the bassinet right, am I already failing her, what if I never feel normal again—and then I’m wide-awake for hours, drifting off just before she wakes up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel that way a lot of the day, most days. It’s like this heaviness I can’t shake, even when nothing specific is wrong. Sometimes I just look at her and feel like I should be happier, but instead I’m just… sad.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

It’s happened a couple of times this week—once when she wouldn’t stop crying and I felt completely helpless, and another time when my partner asked how I was doing and I just burst into tears. I felt like I couldn’t explain it; I just needed to cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’ve had a couple of brief flashes—like when everything feels too much, I’ll think, “What if I just weren’t here?”—but they pass quickly, and I’ve never made any plan or wanted to act on it. I’m more scared of the thought than anything else.

Your words paint a picture of deep postpartum distress-persistent sadness, daily anxiety, and overwhelming guilt that leave you feeling <quote>not yourself</quote>. The intrusive worries, racing heart, and tearful spells show how hard these early weeks have become.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient states she cannot genuinely laugh and nothing seems funny, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only a "tiny spark" of anticipation and avoids planning due to expected lack of enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("a lot") and explicitly links it to motherhood failures, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily worry without real cause, matching 'very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden intense panic attacks multiple times in the week with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and physical anxiety symptoms, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of insomnia driven by intrusive worries, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "a lot of the day, most days" matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two distinct crying episodes this week triggered by feeling overwhelmed and helpless, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent passive suicidal ideation ('brief flashes' of not wanting to be here) that arise 'sometimes' when overwhelmed, matching the frequency and intensity of the 'Sometimes' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 indicates high probability of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Patient meets ≥5 <med>DSM-5</med> criteria: depressed mood most days (<sym>heaviness</sym>), markedly diminished interest (<sym>nothing seems funny</sym>), fatigue, guilt, concentration worries, sleep disturbance, and recurrent passive suicidal thoughts. Anxiety items are also maximally endorsed, suggesting comorbid <med>peripartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day safety assessment and diagnostic evaluation with ob-gyn or PCP
2. Request formal suicide-risk interview using Columbia Scale; involve support person if patient agrees
3. Consider initiation of evidence-based treatment (therapy, medication) tailored to breastfeeding status
4. Provide 24/7 crisis numbers and schedule follow-up within 48 hours
5. Offer immediate support: practical help at home, sleep breaks, peer group referral
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style inquiry):

<sym>Depressed mood, anhedonia</sym>: persistent sadness, inability to experience pleasure or humor, “heaviness most of the day, most days.”  
<sym>Excessive self-blame / guilt</sym>: attributes infant fussiness to personal failure; “I’m not a good mom.”  
<sym>Generalized & catastrophic anxiety</sym>: daily “hum of worry,” intrusive fears for baby’s safety.  
<sym>Panic episodes</sym>: chest tightness, breathlessness, dread “a few times this week” without triggers.  
<sym>Feeling overwhelmed</sym>: “drowning in little tasks,” difficulty coping with routine infant care/household duties.  
<sym>Sleep-onset difficulty linked to rumination</sym>: lies awake for hours worrying, then awake with baby.  
<sym>Crying spells</sym>: twice this week, provoked by infant crying or partner inquiry.  
<sym>Passive self-harm ideation</sym>: brief “what if I weren’t here” thoughts, no plan or intent; patient finds thoughts distressing.

Pattern: High endorsement of affective, cognitive, and anxiety items; low pleasure; functional impairment with infant care; passive suicidal ideation present.

Screening significance: findings exceed threshold for probable <med>major depressive episode with peripartum onset</med> and comorbid <med>anxiety</med>; passive SI warrants immediate safety/risk assessment.

Next steps: Recommend formal diagnostic evaluation, suicide-risk interview, and discussion of treatment/support options today.
